entities.summary:
The Battle of Dunkirk was a pivotal event in World War II, occurring between May 26th and June 4th, 1940, where Allied forces evacuated over 338,000 soldiers from the beaches of Dunkirk, France, marking a significant turning point in the war.

The battle began in earnest when German forces, led by General Gerd von Rundstedt, launched a massive assault on the Dunkirk perimeter, intent on capturing the strategic port city and crippling the Allied war effort.

Despite being vastly outnumbered and outgunned, the Allied forces, led by Lord Gort, held their ground, employing innovative tactics and sheer determination to hold off the German army.

As the battle raged on, the Allies were forced to retreat to the beaches, where a flotilla of ships and boats, including naval vessels and civilian vessels, evacuated the troops in a daring and chaotic operation.

The evacuation, code-named 'Operation Dynamo,' was a testament to the ingenuity and resilience of the Allied forces, who managed to rescue over 338,000 soldiers, saving them from certain capture and death.

The Battle of Dunkirk had far-reaching consequences, galvanizing the Allied war effort and giving new hope to the British people, who had been reeling from a series of crushing defeats.

In the aftermath of the battle, Winston Churchill famously declared, 'We shall fight on the beaches, in the streets, in the fields and in the hills. We shall never surrender,' a rallying cry that would become a defining moment of the war.

The battle's most enduring legacy is the creation of the 'Little Ships,' a fleet of boats and ships that played a crucial role in the evacuation, many of which would go on to serve as a symbol of British resilience and determination.
